newsitem.title: INDIA: India president demands proof of stable government.
newsitem.headline: India president demands proof of stable government.

text.p: India's president on Sunday told the country's bickering politicians to prove that a new centre-left alliance would be more stable than its predecessor before he would ask it to form a government.

President Shankar Dayal Sharma made the demand to Congress party president Sitaram Kesri, who met him after the ousted United Front alliance elected a new leader to succeed caretaker Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and staked a claim to form a new governmnent.
Congress politicians said Kesri renewed his party's offer of support for United Front prime minister-in-waiting Inder Kumar Gujral. But the president was apparently not impressed.

"President Sharma has asked the Congress party to show reliable proof that the new government will not be an unstable one," a senior Congress official told Reuters after a meeting of the party's policy-making Congress Working Committee (CWC).

Congress politicians said their leaders were also holding talks with the Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) party, whose leader G.K. Moopanar was passed over as a United Front candidate for the top job in preference for Gujral.
The TMC subsequently decided against joining a new government but offered to remain a member of the United Front.

The United Front has 178 deputies in the 545-seat lower house of parliament. Congress, which controls 140 deputies, could become numerically stronger than the United Front if Moopanar defected with his 20 deputies, Congress politicians said.
"Basically, we want to have bargaining strength vis-a-vis the United Front," one CWC member said. "With the TMC's current position, we have become stronger."
Congress officials said Sharma had asked that Congress and the United Front establish a mechanism for ensuring that the next government is a stable one.

Kesri's withdrawal of support for Deve Gowda forced the government to resign on April 11 after it was defeated in a vote of confidence jointly by the Congress and its rightwing Hindu opponent, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which has 194 deputies in parliament.

Earlier on Sunday, parliamentarians from the 15-party alliance elected 77-year-old Gujral as their leader, endorsing the choice made late on Saturday by the alliance's decision-making Steering Committee.
Alliance leader Chandrababu Naidu told reporters he expected Sharma to invite Gujral later on Sunday to head the government.
"We have staked a claim to form the government," Naidu said. "We are hopeful of forming the government very soon."
But Sharma's message to Kesri dampened that hope.
United Front officials said the alliance was holding a meeting of the Steering Committee to seek to resolve the stalemate.
A communist member of the Steering Committee said the alliance was prepared to discuss policy-making with the Congress.
"But there is no way we can entertain Congress policies if they go against our own."
